The striped polecat (Ictonyx striatus) exhibits a life history strategy typical of small, solitary mustelids inhabiting sub-Saharan African savannas. Neonates emerge from the reproductive tract after a gestation period of thirty-six days [tg = thirty-six days], a duration that is relatively short for a mustelid of this size and likely reflects the energetic constraints of the female's carnivorous diet, measured at a core body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. The wet weight at birth is a mere 15 grams [Wwb = 15 grams], placing newborn kits among the smallest relative to adult size within the Ictonychinae subfamily. This altricial state necessitates intense maternal investment during the early post-natal phase, during which offspring remain fully dependent on the female for thermoregulation and nutrition. The species is monovular, producing one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], a low reproductive frequency that is consistent with a slow life-history pace. Each litter contains two offspring [N_R_i = Each litter contains two offspring], a modest litter size that aligns with the constraints of carnivorous lactation, as provisioning two rapidly growing kits imposes substantial metabolic demands on the mother while she maintains her own body condition at 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C].

By this stage, kits have grown considerably from their 15-gram (15 grams) [Wwb = 15 grams] neonatal mass, reaching a wet weight at weaning of approximately 170 grams [Wwx = approximately 170 grams], representing an elevenfold increase in just over eleven weeks. This period of rapid somatic growth is fueled by the female's intensive hunting efforts; she must capture sufficient small vertebrates and invertebrates to both sustain her own metabolic demands at 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C] and provision her offspring as they approach nutritional independence. Weaning coincides with the onset of exploratory behavior, as the young begin to accompany the mother on foraging excursions and progressively develop the predatory skills necessary for independent survival in the mosaic of grassland and scrub that constitutes their typical habitat.

Sexual maturation in the striped polecat occurs at different ages for males and females, a pattern of protandrous development seen in many mustelids. Under the standard thermal regime of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], the time since birth at puberty for males is 393 days [tp = 393 days], approximately thirteen months after birth, while females reach reproductive maturity somewhat earlier, at 304 days [tp = 304 days]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation timing likely reflects the differing selective pressures acting on each sex: males may require a longer growth period to attain the body size necessary for successful competition with conspecifics during the breeding season, whereas females can afford to mature earlier and begin producing litters at a younger age. The delayed male maturation may also be linked to the species' solitary, polygynous mating system, in which larger, older males are typically more successful in securing access to receptive females. Both sexes continue to increase in mass throughout this prolonged juvenile phase, gradually approaching the asymptotic adult dimensions that characterize fully reproductively competent individuals.

Adult individuals of Ictonyx striatus are among the larger members of the African polecat group. The ultimate wet weight, or maximum recorded adult body mass, is approximately 910 grams [Wwi = approximately 910 grams], a value that places this species at the upper end of the size range for the genus. This substantial body mass is supported by an elongated, robustly muscled trunk and relatively short limbs, an adaptation for pursuing prey through burrow systems and dense ground cover. Adults maintain a core temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C] during active periods, a typical eutherian value that reflects the metabolic demands of a carnivorous, actively foraging predator inhabiting a warm, semi-arid environment. The pelage, a striking pattern of white stripes on a black background, serves as an aposematic signal to potential predators, advertising the species' potent anal gland secretions. Compared to related mustelids of similar body mass, such as the zorilla, the striped polecat exhibits a relatively high surface-area-to-volume ratio that may influence its thermoregulatory costs, though the dense fur provides substantial insulation during cooler nocturnal hours.

Longevity data for the striped polecat are derived primarily from captive records and limited field observations. The maximum recorded lifespan in captivity is 14 years [am = 14 years], measured at a stable core temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], a duration that is remarkable for a mammal of this body size and places it among the longer-lived mustelids relative to its mass. This extended lifespan is associated with a slow reproductive pace, as females produce only a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year] of two cubs per litter [N_R_i = two cubs per litter], resulting in a low maximum annual reproductive rate. Natural mortality in the wild is likely much higher, driven by predation, intraspecific aggression, and resource limitation in the seasonal African landscape. The combination of a relatively long life, extended juvenile period with delayed maturity in males, and low fecundity suggests that Ictonyx striatus follows a conservative life-history trajectory, prioritizing adult survival over high reproductive output in the face of unpredictable environmental conditions typical of its savanna and grassland ecosystems.
